b.x: Evasion protocol. Gray man. Extreme chaos. Central philosophy: be unseen, light, and adaptable. Do not be a target, do not call attention, survive and leave. What the gray man is. Someone who does not stand out: no uniforms, no visible marks, no flashy goods. He passes unnoticed in any crowd. In extreme chaos, that is his greatest advantage. What to carry. Golden rules. Rule 1: everything must fit in one discreet pack. No large bags or suitcases. Rule 2: if it is not essential, leave it. Weight is death. Rule 3: everything should be gray, black, beige, no prints, no brands. Minimum kit, in order of priority. Immediate survival. Water: one tough bottle and purification tablets. Light, and they go far. Food: only food that does not spoil, is light, and has no smell. Cereal bars, dried fruit, biscuits. No cans. Heavy and noisy. A filter mask or a cotton cloth, and simple glasses. Dust, smoke, gas. A lighter or waterproof matches, and one small candle. Health and protection. A compact first-aid kit: dressings, gauze, antiseptic, pain relief, essential personal medicines. Strong tape and a simple blade or pocket knife. Cash, small notes, hidden in different places, and the minimum papers in protected plastic. Navigation and communication. A printed map of the region. Phones may not work. A small whistle. A signal without spending the voice. A small flashlight with red light. It does not draw attention. Use it only in an emergency. Clothes and extras. One full change of clothes, neutral colors. A light layer and a rain cover that folds small. Shoes already on: comfortable and worn. Never new. What not to carry. Jewelry, expensive watches, visible electronics. Visible weapons. They make you an immediate target. Too many clothes. Unnecessary weight. Food with a strong smell. It draws people and animals. What to be prepared to face. Insecurity and conflict. Looting and hostile groups: avoid crowds. If someone stops you, do not resist. Hand over what they ask. Your life is worth more than your belongings. Crossfire: always walk close to walls, behind barriers. Never run across open ground. Stay below the line of sight. False helpers: not everyone who offers help is trustworthy. Trust your instincts. If something feels wrong, move away in silence. Lack of basic resources. Without water or food: do not drink water from an unknown source without purifying it. Eat little and slowly. Thirst is more urgent than hunger. A human lasts about three days without water, and weeks without food. Without electricity and without communication: do not depend on a phone. Batteries die fast. Memorize paths and landmarks. Without shelter: be willing to sleep in simple places. Stairs, corridors, trees. What matters is to be off the street and hidden. Environmental and health dangers. Unbreathable air: dust, smoke, toxic gases. Breathe through a wet cloth. Stay in higher areas if there is smoke. Wounds and illness: small cuts can infect. Wash whenever you can. Avoid contact with sick people. Cold, heat, and rain: hypothermia kills faster than hunger. Stay dry. Psychological challenges. Fear and panic: panic makes you commit grave errors. Breathe deep. Walk slowly. Think before you act. Solitude and distrust: too much trust is dangerous, but total distrust also isolates. Watch first, decide after. Extreme fatigue: rest in short, safe intervals. Do not push yourself to exhaustion. You will need energy for what comes. Golden rules of evasion. One. Leave before it is too late. The window is short. Hesitation is getting trapped. Two. Less is more. The less you carry, the faster you move and the less attention you draw. Three. Be unseen. Do not hold eye contact, do not answer provocations, do not make noise. Be part of the scenery. Four. Keep moving, but with discretion. Running is a target. Walking fast is a clear destination. Five. Always have two routes. If the first is blocked, you already know the alternative. Six. Do not trust anyone completely, but be polite with everyone. Kindness costs nothing and can save your life. Seven. Arriving matters more than arriving first. The one who wins is not the one who leaves first. It is the one who arrives alive. Last word. The gray man is not a hero. He is not a soldier. He is someone who simply wants to survive and begin again. His greatest strength is not in what he carries, but in how he thinks and stays calm when everything around him falls.
